name: Design a Large Email Service
intent: Send hundreds of millions of messages a day without being throttled or blocklisted, and receive, filter, store and search the mail for a hundred million mailboxes.
codeTitle: an outbound scheduler with per-domain queues
finalIntro: One campaign message going out, and one reply coming back in.
prompt: Design an email service that both sends and receives mail at large scale. Customers send campaigns and receipts to millions of addresses at many providers. The same service hosts mailboxes for a hundred million users, who expect new mail within seconds, no spam, and fast search over years of messages.
functional: Accept messages to send through an API or SMTP, and deliver them to the recipient's mail server
Retry temporary failures, and stop sending to addresses that bounce permanently
Sign outgoing mail so receivers can verify it, and check the same on incoming mail
Receive mail for hosted domains, filter spam and put the rest in the right mailbox
Store each user's mail for years, and let them list, read and search it
Report delivered, deferred, bounced and complaint counts per campaign
nonFunctional: Several hundred million messages sent per day, with big campaigns that arrive as a sudden burst
Respect each receiving provider's limits, since going too fast gets the sender throttled and then blocklisted
A message is never lost once accepted, and is sent to the recipient at least once and almost never twice
New mail is searchable and visible within a few seconds
Spam complaints stay below the level providers punish, which is a rate under about 0.1%
Mailbox reads under 100 ms, and years of mail per user at a low cost per gigabyte

firstAttempt.text: One mail server, such as Postfix, on one IP address. Applications hand it messages and it opens an SMTP connection to the recipient's server for each one, in the order they arrived. Incoming mail is written to files on the same machine, and search is a scan of those files.
limits: A big campaign goes out as fast as the server can manage, so a provider that accepts only a few messages a minute answers with errors, then slows or blocks the sender
A slow or failing provider holds up the messages queued behind it for other providers
Failed messages are retried straight away or dropped, and addresses that do not exist are mailed again every time
The messages are not signed, so receivers cannot tell them from forgeries and many land in spam
One IP address carries all the reputation, so one bad campaign damages all mail, including receipts
Everything lives on one machine: no filtering of incoming spam, no redundancy, and searching years of mail means reading every file

steps.title: Queue the mail, with one queue per receiving domain
steps.problem: Sending in arrival order ignores that every provider has its own limits. A campaign of ten million messages is mostly for a few big providers and a long tail of small servers, and one shared queue treats them all the same.
steps.fix: The Send API accepts the message, stores it durably and puts it on a queue named after the recipient's domain, such as gmail.com. A pool of outbound mail transfer agents (MTAs) pulls from each queue at that domain's own rate: a limit on messages per minute and on open connections, tuned from the answers the domain gives. A domain that answers 421 or 451, meaning slow down, gets a lower rate, and a domain that accepts everything is allowed to speed up. A slow domain only delays its own queue.
steps.tradeoff: One slow or strict provider no longer holds up the others, and the sender stays inside each provider's limits, which protects its reputation. There are many queues to manage and rates to tune, and the biggest domains need to be split further, for example by sending IP, since one limit per domain is not enough for them.

steps.title: Retry temporary failures, and suppress permanent ones
steps.problem: A refused message is either a temporary problem (the mailbox is full, the server is busy, greylisting) or a permanent one (the address does not exist). Treating both alike either loses good mail or keeps mailing dead addresses, which providers count against the sender.
steps.fix: SMTP separates them by the reply code: 4xx is temporary and 5xx is permanent. A 4xx puts the message back on its domain queue with a delay that grows after each failure, with some random spread, so a recovered provider is not hit by everything at once. Real systems start at a few minutes and give up after about four or five days, and then send a failure notice to the sender. A 5xx hard bounce is final: the bounce processor adds the address to the suppression list, and the Send API refuses to queue anything for it from then on.
steps.tradeoff: Good mail survives a provider's bad hour and dead addresses stop costing reputation. Retries make delivery slower and the queues bigger, and a suppression list must be shared by all of a customer's campaigns, kept for a long time and have a way to remove an address once the owner asks.

steps.title: Sign every message, and warm up each new IP
steps.problem: Receivers cannot know that a message from your domain is really from you, so forged mail is easy and real mail is distrusted. A new IP address has no history either, and a big volume from an unknown address looks just like spam.
steps.fix: Outgoing mail passes through a signing step. SPF is a DNS record that lists the IPs allowed to send for a domain. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to the message headers that the receiver checks with a public key published in DNS. DMARC is a DNS policy that says what to do with mail that fails both, such as quarantine or reject, and where to send reports. New IPs go through a warm-up schedule that starts at a small daily volume to engaged recipients and grows by about half each day, over weeks. Transactional mail such as receipts uses a different pool from bulk marketing.
steps.tradeoff: Providers accept the mail and attackers cannot easily impersonate the domain, and a bad campaign cannot damage receipts. Keys must be rotated and kept safe, DNS records have to match what is sent, and warm-up is slow: a sudden need for ten times the volume cannot be met in a day.

steps.title: Receive mail, and filter spam in stages
steps.problem: Most inbound mail is spam, and accepting all of it costs storage and delivers abuse to users. Checking every message deeply, though, is expensive, and a wrong decision on a good message loses real mail.
steps.fix: Inbound SMTP servers accept connections and run cheap checks first, while the sender is still connected: is the IP on a blocklist, does SPF pass, is the DKIM signature valid, what does the sender's DMARC policy say, and is the sender sending too fast. Mail that survives goes to the spam filter stage, which scores it with content rules and a trained model, and uses the sender's history. A high score is rejected during the SMTP conversation, so the sender gets a bounce, a middle score goes to the spam folder, and the rest to the inbox. Rejecting is better than accepting and discarding, since a bounce to a forged address would go to an innocent person.
steps.tradeoff: Most spam is stopped before it costs anything, and good mail is accepted quickly. The scoring can be wrong in both directions, so the spam folder must be searchable and the system must learn from users' reports, and the cheap early checks must be fast enough not to slow the SMTP conversation.

steps.title: Store mail in a mailbox store, with a separate search index
steps.problem: A single mail file or directory per user does not scale to years of mail, and a scan of it makes search take minutes. Attachments are large, and identical ones arrive in thousands of mailboxes.
steps.fix: Each message body and attachment is written once to an object store, addressed by a hash of its content. A sharded mailbox database keeps the small, hot metadata per user: folder, flags, subject, date and a pointer to the body, sharded by user id so a whole mailbox is on one shard. Listing the inbox is a range read on that shard. A search index, also sharded by user, receives each new message through a queue and keeps an inverted index of its terms, so a search for a word finds a user's messages without reading them. The indexing runs in the background, so a message appears in a few seconds.
steps.tradeoff: Listing and reading are fast, bodies are stored cheaply and shared copies are stored once. There are three stores to keep consistent, and search can lag a few seconds behind delivery. Deleting a message must also remove its postings from the index and its bodies when no one refers to them.

steps.title: Watch reputation and feed it back into the sending rate
steps.problem: Reputation is slow to build and quick to lose, and the signals arrive late: complaints, bounce rates, blocklist listings and DMARC reports. A campaign can damage the IPs before anyone looks at a dashboard.
steps.fix: A reputation monitor combines the signals per IP pool, per sending domain and per receiving provider: the share of hard bounces, the number of 421 and 451 replies, spam complaints from feedback loops, blocklist status and the aggregated DMARC reports. It reduces the send rate for a pool when a signal passes its threshold, pauses a campaign that crosses an error budget, and alerts a person. Customers with a bounce or complaint rate above the limit are slowed, then suspended.
steps.tradeoff: A bad list is caught within minutes, which limits the damage to a pool to a small part of one campaign. The thresholds will sometimes slow a good campaign, they need tuning per provider, and an abusive customer can still do some harm before they are caught.

failures.scenario: A big provider starts answering 421 to everything
failures.impact: Its queue grows quickly, and if the system retried at full speed it would be blocked for a long time.
failures.answer: The domain's rate drops as the 421 replies arrive and its messages wait in their own queue with growing delays. Other domains are not affected. When the provider recovers the rate rises again slowly, and the oldest messages are sent first. A message that is still undelivered after the retry window gets a failure notice.

failures.scenario: The IP appears on a blocklist
failures.impact: Receivers reject the mail with a 550, and the messages look like normal bounces, so retries make it worse.
failures.answer: The monitor recognises blocklist rejections by their text and by a sudden jump in 5xx replies from many providers, and stops sending from that IP. Traffic is moved to other IPs in the pool, the cause is found (usually a bad list or a compromised account), and the listing is requested to be removed. Messages are held, not bounced, while it is fixed.

failures.scenario: The same message is delivered twice
failures.impact: A worker sent a message and crashed before it recorded that it had, so the retry sends it again.
failures.answer: Delivery is at least once, since losing a mail is worse than a duplicate. The window is made small by recording the result as soon as the server answers 250, and each message has a unique id that is also placed in the Message-ID header so the recipient's own filters can recognise a repeat. Receipts that must not be duplicated use a dedupe key on the Send API.

failures.scenario: A customer uploads an old list with a lot of dead addresses
failures.impact: A wave of hard bounces and spam complaints damages the reputation of the shared IPs.
failures.answer: The first bounces reach the monitor within minutes, and the campaign is paused when its hard-bounce rate passes the threshold, typically about 2 to 5 percent. The bounced addresses are suppressed, and the customer is asked to clean the list, usually by sending only to addresses that have been active recently. Repeat offenders are moved to a separate pool or suspended.

failures.scenario: A search index shard is lost
failures.impact: Search for the users on that shard returns nothing, while their mail is still fine.
failures.answer: The mailbox store is the source of truth and the index is derived from it. A replica takes over, and the rest is rebuilt by reading the shard's mailboxes again and re-indexing, one user at a time, with the most recently active users first. Until then the app shows recent mail from the metadata, and search is marked as incomplete.

alternatives.title: How to limit the sending rate

options.name: One global rate
options.pro: Trivial to build and to explain
options.con: Too fast for small providers and too slow for large ones, so it triggers throttling and wastes capacity at once

options.name: A queue and a limit per receiving domain
options.pro: Each provider gets what it will take, and a slow one holds up only itself
options.con: More queues, and the limits need tuning and learning from the replies

options.name: Per domain and per sending IP
options.pro: Fits how large providers actually judge reputation, which is per IP and per domain
options.con: Needs IP pools and a scheduler that knows both

alternatives.pick: A queue per receiving domain, with limits that adapt from the replies, and a split by sending IP for the largest providers.

alternatives.title: How to retry

options.name: No retries
options.con: Every temporary error becomes a lost message

options.name: Fixed short interval
options.pro: Quick delivery when the problem was brief
options.con: Hammers a provider that is already refusing, which counts against the sender

options.name: Exponential backoff with jitter, and a limit of days
options.pro: Gentle on the receiver, and delivers once the problem is over
options.con: Slow for a message that needed only a short wait, and the queues hold many waiting messages

alternatives.pick: Exponential backoff with jitter, starting at minutes and stopping after a few days.

alternatives.title: Where mail bodies live

options.name: Files per user (Maildir)
options.pro: Simple and robust, and easy to back up
options.con: Millions of small files per server, no sharing of attachments and slow search

options.name: Metadata in a database, bodies in an object store
options.pro: Fast listing, cheap storage and deduplicated attachments
options.con: Two systems to keep in step

options.name: Everything in one database
options.con: Large bodies make the database big and expensive

alternatives.pick: Metadata in a sharded database, and bodies and attachments in an object store.

alternatives.title: What to do with likely spam

options.name: Reject during SMTP
options.pro: No storage cost, and the sender sees the failure
options.con: A false positive loses a good message, and a forged sender receives a useless bounce

options.name: Accept and put in a spam folder
options.pro: Nothing is lost, and the user can rescue it
options.con: Storage cost and some spam reaches the user

alternatives.pick: Reject what is certainly spam during SMTP, and file the uncertain middle in a spam folder.
